research.abstract: Centromeres are essential for chromosome function, yet how contrasting centromere architectures shape polyploid genome evolution and plant diversification remains unresolved. In monocentric chromosomes, centromeric activity is restricted to one chromosomal region; in holocentric chromosomes, it is distributed along the chromosome length. Hybridization followed by genome doubling can place chromosome sets with different centromeres, repeat complements, and rearrangement histories in the same nucleus. We examined whether such genomic mergers are associated with later chromosome restructuring in carnivorous Caryophyllales, focusing on chromosome-scale assemblies of putatively holocentric Drosera regia and monocentric D. capensis. The two sundews retain broad syntenic continuity and related polyploid ancestry, but their present genomes differ sharply. D. regia preserves several ancestral chromosomal fusions and dispersed candidate centromere-associated satellite repeats, whereas D. capensis has stronger internal duplication, extensive rearrangement, and localized centromeres. Phylogenomic and structural analyses suggest a reticulate evolutionary history for D. regia, with part of its genome showing preferential structural affinity to the Venus flytrap lineage. Whereas D. regia exhibits threefold syntenic depth consistent with hexaploidy, D. capensis exhibits sixfold depth consistent with dodecaploidy, and structural comparisons do not support simple doubling of the extant D. regia-like architecture. Repeat profiling across a broad sample of Drosera also shows rapid turnover and species-level differences in centromere-associated DNA. These results place centromere organization alongside polyploid history and chromosome restructuring as a major axis of genome evolution in sundews.

research.abstract: Bayesian phylogenetic inference produces large samples from a posterior distribution over phylogenetic trees that represents uncertainty in both tree topology and associated variables. Such a collection of trees is hard to interpret and it is common practice to summarize such samples into a single representative tree.Methods for constructing representative trees have largely been restricted to plain tree topologies, encoding only relationships among taxa. Inference with more sophisticated models produce annotated tree objects. These have additional information representing nodes' locations in the case of phylogeography, host information when inferring transmission trees, or sampled ancestor status when incorporating fossil information. Nevertheless, these annotated representations are reduced to a single representative tree, typically using methods developed for plain tree topologies and without accounting for the resulting methodological mismatch.Here, we introduce the concept of an extended clade and investigate an extension of the conditional clade distribution (CCD) model. Through motivating examples and case studies in discrete trait phylogeography and transmission tree reconstruction, we demonstrate limitations of standard summary tree approaches and show how these can be addressed using an extended CCD framework that explicitly incorporates the annotated tree structure.

research.abstract: Forecasting the evolution of viral proteins can help inform pandemic preparedness and guide the development of interventions. Phylogenetic trees provide historical records of pathogen evolution, which are key for retrospective analysis, but using them to predict future genotypic changes remains challenging. We introduce antiGen, a machine learning model that learns from the evolutionary past of viruses to forecast the evolutionary future. antiGen achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting SARS-CoV-2 spike protein mutations according to a variety of metrics, including the prediction of mutations in the receptor binding domain, mutations never previously seen, and mutations with high prevalence. Most experimentally tested antiGen-forecasted spike variants retain pseudoviral infectivity in vitro, supporting their functional plausibility. Evaluations on surface proteins of influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and dengue virus further demonstrate applicability across viruses with differing amounts of available sequencing data. Finally, we develop a model trained across 49 viral proteins from 27 viruses, which improves forecasting performance over models trained on individual protein phylogenies. Together, these results support learning from phylogenetic histories as an approach to model viral amino acid changes prospectively, with applications in epidemiology and therapeutic development.

research.abstract: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC chains with known ESS bounds. We compare existing tree ESS estimators with novel approaches that utilize CCDs as tractable tree distributions, as well as a new probabilistic estimator based on differences in clade frequencies between independent chains. Using our emulated chains from both simulated and real datasets, we assess estimators for their ability to recover the true ESS (accuracy), their insensitivity to the removal of autocorrelated samples from the chain (stability), and their tolerance to combining multiple chains together (robustness). We further examine how multimodality and poor inter-mode chain mixing can compromise the reliability of tree ESS estimates. These findings indicate that our new CCD-based estimators perform comparably to existing approaches with respect to accuracy, stability, and robustness. In contrast, the probabilistic estimator and two previously recommended methods incur prohibitive computational costs for long chains. Together, these results establish a new framework for evaluating tree ESS estimators using CCD-based emulated MCMC chains and demonstrate their performance and current limitations in practical phylogenetic analyses. The expanded suite of tree ESS estimators is available in the user-friendly TreeStat2 software package for BEAST 2.

research.abstract: Objective Evidence on inpatient-related costs for tuberculosis (TB) patients remains limited for Southwest China. This study used quantile regression to explore factors associated with inpatient expenditures among TB patients treated at a designated infectious-disease hospital in Guizhou Province, Southwest China. Methods Baseline characteristics and inpatient cost data of TB patients admitted to a designated infectious disease hospital in Guizhou Province from January 2018 to December 2024 were retrospectively collected. Quantile regression models were applied to identify determinants of inpatient costs across different cost distributions. Results The findings showed that, at lower cost quantiles, self pay patients had lower inpatient costs (10th percentile; coefficient = -141.79). Conversely, patients covered by social basic medical insurance had significantly lower inpatient costs at higher cost quantiles (90th percentile; coefficient = -97 404.08). Manual labor workers and retirees had higher inpatient costs across the 10th to 90th percentiles compared with other occupational groups. Inpatient length of stay, receipt of interventional procedures, drug resistance, admission status, and comorbidities were positively associated with inpatient costs across the 10th to 90th percentiles (all P < 0.001). Cost differences existed across quantiles for different TB types: disseminated TB produced the highest costs at the 10th percentile (coefficient = 1367.35), while tuberculous meningitis incurred the highest costs from the 50th to the 90th percentiles. According to the relative importance ranking, the most influential factors (in descending order) were length of stay, admission status, TB type, procedural intervention, and occupational factors. Conclusion Based on seven year consecutive inpatient data, this study indicates that TB inpatient expenditures are affected by multiple factors and differ across cost quantiles. Targeted cost containment strategies should be developed according to patient characteristics to reduce medical expenses and shorten hospital stays without impairing treatment outcomes. These findings provide theoretical evidence for formulating TB cost control policies for similar hospital settings. Caution should be exercised when generalizing these results to all TB patients across Southwest China given the single center study design.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates. Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis. Methods P. aeruginosa ( n= 137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification. Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns. Results High AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant. AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%). Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections. Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]). No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified. AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering. Conclusions Our study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians with bronchiectasis. High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this neglected clinical cohort.

research.abstract: Abstract Background TB eradication strategies in high burden countries need affordable, scalable, and accessible screening tools. This study investigated the diagnostic accuracy of C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid A (SAA), and interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10) as potential screening tools. Method This cross-sectional diagnostic study investigated stored archived serum samples from three groups of subjects; bacteriology confirmed symptomatic TB group (n=57), probable TB (n=56) and healthy controls (n=60). CRP and SAA concentrations were measured using near point-of-care fluorescence immunoassay (NPOCT-FIA), while IP-10 was measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Diagnostic performance of individual and combined biomarkers was evaluated Results Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance of serum amyloid A (SAA) and C-reactive protein (CRP) for identifying confirmed tuberculosis (TB). Compared with probable TB and healthy controls, SAA achieved an AUC of 0.961 (cut-off > 31.0 mg/L), with 96.5% sensitivity and 88.6% specificity, while CRP achieved an AUC of 0.953 (cut-off 21.3 mg/L), with 96.5% sensitivity and 86.0% specificity. Interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10) showed poor discrimination (AUC 0.545). Combined CRP and SAA achieved 100.0% sensitivity and 83.3% specificity. Conclusion SAA and CRP met WHO target product profile criteria for TB triage screening.

research.abstract: Abstract Tarsiers, an elusive family of primates found in Indonesia and the Philippines, sit at an essential point in primate evolution, with their divergence between that of Strepsirrhini (lemurs) and Simiiformes (monkeys and apes). Through homology searches, we have discovered that tarsiers carry the first known case in primates of a gene expansion of protein kinase R (PKR), a kinase involved in the response to viral infection. PKR was quadruplicated in the ancestor of tarsiers and has been maintained since then in all sequenced tarsier species. The extra copies lack the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding domains necessary for detecting viral infection yet largely maintain the residues necessary for the kinase function that carries out PKR’s antiviral function. We show that three of the four PKR copies indeed maintain kinase activity, one of which appears to be resistant to the viral PKR antagonist K3 from vaccinia virus. Our analyses of site and branch-site positive selection reveal that the tarsier PKRs are under positive selection. We propose that these extra copies could serve as a diversification strategy to bypass viral inhibitors that bind PKR’s kinase domain, or they could alternatively serve as decoys that shield the canonical PKR from viral inhibition. This is the first instance of mammal PKR duplicates lacking dsRNA-binding domains and may highlight an innovation in an ancient, long-standing molecular arms race between viruses and a close relative of humans.

research.abstract: Abstract Nishikigoi, ornamental cultivars of the common carp ( Cyprinus carpio ), are economically valuable aquaculture teleosts in which mature females command significantly higher market prices due to superior body conformation and coloration. Consequently, early and non-invasive sex identification is highly desirable for commercial breeding. Although sex determination in common carp follows an XX/XY system, sex-chromosome-specific markers and field-applicable diagnostic methods for Nishikigoi have remained limited. In this study, we conducted sequence-based bulked segregant analysis using whole-genome shotgun sequencing of female and male pools in Kohaku, a representative Nishikigoi lineage. We identified male-specific candidate contigs and successfully developed PCR-based male-specific markers. Validation across multiple Nishikigoi varieties and wild common carp demonstrated that primary primer pairs achieved high diagnostic accuracy. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that these candidate contigs mapped to the genomic region on chromosome 25B containing the male-determining gene Pangu , with the primary marker located in immediate physical proximity to the gene. To enable field diagnostics, we combined non-invasive epidermal mucus DNA extraction, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), and chromatography-printed array strip (C-PAS) technology, establishing a rapid on- site detection workflow. Overall, this study provides highly reliable PCR markers associated with the sex-determination locus and establishes a non-invasive, field-applicable diagnostic platform to streamline commercial Nishikigoi breeding and sex-selected stock management.

research.abstract: Abstract Background The HIV reservoir persists in long-living immune cells after antiretroviral therapy initiation. Proviral DNA integrates at preferential host DNA sites, while HIV transcription continues under treatment, with potential biological consequences. Treated people with HIV remain at increased risk for premature aging and non-AIDS comorbidities compared to people without HIV. Whether HIV reservoir size and activity impact health outcomes during treatment remains unclear. Methods We analyzed 1895 people with HIV using antiretroviral therapy from the 2000HIV cohort to study associations between the reservoir and historic and prospective virologic and immunological response markers, comorbidity outcomes and biological aging scores. The reservoir was assessed by quantifying total and intact proviral HIV DNA in circulating CD4+ T cells, along with measures of HIV transcriptional activity, including cell-associated HIV RNA. Results HIV reservoir markers were highly correlating and associated with older aging scores and adverse virologic outcomes, including quantifiable and residual viremia at study entry and during follow-up. Total HIV DNA, unlike the minor fraction of intact HIV DNA, correlated with prevalent cardiovascular disease, subclinical atherosclerotic disease, liver fibrosis and incident malignancies independent of circulating inflammatory markers and lowest CD4 nadir. Total HIV RNA associated with prevalent cardiovascular disease and liver fibrosis. Conclusion The HIV reservoir associated with older aging scores and long-term health outcomes in people with HIV using antiretroviral therapy, independent of inflammation and immune suppression history. Whether reservoir-reducing interventions lower the risk of non-AIDS comorbidities should be studied in people with high reservoir markers. Funding and trial registration ViiV Healthcare; 2000HIV ClinicalTrials.gov number: NTC03994835 Graphic summary Highlights HIV reservoir markers in circulating CD4 cells, including total and intact HIV DNA as well as total and unspliced HIV RNA, are highly correlated and show largely overlapping clinical and immunological characteristics. People with less favourable HIV clinical phenotypes before ART show higher levels of all measured HIV reservoir markers. Higher total HIV DNA and total HIV RNA associate with older biological aging scores and higher non-AIDS comorbidities risk after start ART. The effect of the reservoir on comorbidities is not purely dependent on systemic inflammation

research.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains the most economically devastating pathogen of the global swine industry, with frequent genetic recombination and continuous lineage replacement driving its rapid evolution. Hubei Province, a major swine-producing hub in central China, endures substantial PRRSV disease pressure, yet the current epidemiological and evolutionary landscape of circulating strains remains poorly characterized. In this study, 1478 clinical samples were collected from 12 prefecture-level cities between 2024 and 2025 and subjected to RT-PCR detection, ORF5 sequencing, virus isolation, and complete genome analysis. The detection rate among clinical samples was 26.32%, highest in nursery pigs (32.65%). Phylogenetic analysis of 136 ORF5 sequences revealed lineage 1 dominance (66.18%), comprising NADC30-like (38.24%) and NADC34-like (27.94%) strains, followed by lineage 8 (24.26%), lineage 5 (5.15%), and lineage 3 (4.41%). Six isolates were recovered, and whole-genome analysis identified lineage-specific NSP2 deletion patterns and a recombinant strain (LW HP) bearing a JXA1-like backbone with NADC30-like insertions. Selection pressure analysis ranked Nsp2 as the least-constrained gene (dN/dS = 0.3065; purifying selection), with positively selected codons in GP5 and the NSP2 hypervariable region. These findings delineate the current epidemic status and genetic characteristics of PRRSV in central China, providing critical data for regional prevention and vaccine development.

research.abstract: Background: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) remains the most lethal central nervous system (CNS) infection in neurosurgical practice, with case fatality rates of 25–50% despite appropriate therapy. Up to 80% of TBM patients develop hydrocephalus, and outcomes in advanced disease are determined primarily by the timing of anti-tuberculous therapy (ATT) rather than the method of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion. We report a fatal case of isolated CNS tuberculosis (TB) complicated by aqueductal stenosis-induced obstructive hydrocephalus, in which a systemic diagnostic delay, driven by the requirement for microbiological confirmation before ATT could be dispensed, cascaded into delayed medical and surgical management and was the principal determinant of outcome rather than surgical technique. Case Description: A 26-year-old human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-negative Egyptian male presented with recurrent high-grade fever, neck stiffness, diplopia, and urinary retention. CSF showed high protein (306.7 mg/ dL), low glucose (42.1 mg/dL), and lymphocytic pleocytosis (400 cells/mm 3 ), with negative Ziehl–Neelsen stain and BioFire ME panel, which does not include Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). Despite a CSF profile suggestive of TBM, GeneXpert MTB/rifampicin Ultra was not performed and ATT was deferred pending polymerase chain reaction confirmation. Dexamethasone was started appropriately on day 1. Computed tomography (CT) brain showed ventricular dilatation, but neurosurgical consultation was not obtained. CT chest later showed no pulmonary involvement, supporting isolated CNS TB. On Day 5, the patient deteriorated to Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 6–7 with seizures; emergency external ventricular drain (EVD) was inserted and ATT initiated on day 6, approximately 36 days after symptom onset. He subsequently developed steroid-induced diabetic ketoacidosis and severe hypernatremia consistent with central diabetes insipidus. Despite EVD and ATT, neurological status progressed to GCS 2T with absent brainstem reflexes, and he died approximately 10 days after EVD insertion. Conclusion: This case illustrates three critical failures: (1) neurosurgical consultation was reactive rather than proactive – initiated upon seizures and coma rather than upon CT evidence of hydrocephalus; (2) CSF diversion without concurrent ATT is temporizing, not curative – ongoing meningeal inflammation will progress regardless of EVD adequacy; and (3) a negative syndromic molecular panel that lacks MTB coverage must not delay empirical ATT when the CSF profile is unambiguous. The EVD was technically appropriate and correctly positioned; the therapeutic window had already closed before surgery was performed. In Medical Research Council Grade III TBM, outcome is determined by ATT timing and disease severity at presentation, not by the specific method of CSF diversion.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Positive selection shapes protein function by favoring amino acid substitutions that increase fitness. Although numerous studies have identified positively selected genes (PSGs), the structural principles underlying residue-level positive selection remain incompletely understood and previous studies have produced conflicting conclusions, particularly regarding the preferential location of positively selected residues (PSRs) within intrinsically disordered regions. In order to resolve these issues and to better understand the driving forces underlying positive selection in human proteins, we performed a comprehensive analysis on a manually curated, high quality collection of PSGs and PSRs as well as on a large-scale PSR dataset restricted to proteins with experimental structures. Results Human PSRs were significantly enriched in secreted and cell membrane proteins and preferentially localized to extracellular regions, solvent-exposed protein surfaces, coil structures, and protein-protein interaction interfaces, whereas neither domains nor intrinsically disordered regions showed an enrichment. Spatial clustering analysis reinforced that PSRs accumulate within localized surface patches. Integration of host-pathogen interaction data highlighted that adaptive changes preferentially affect extracellular molecular recognition surfaces, recurrently appearing in certain pathogen-interacting membrane protein families and particular domain types. Additionally, PSRs showed an enrichment in the residues of human-pathogen interaction interfaces that are in direct contact with pathogenic proteins, implying that neutralizing pathogen attacks is one of the driving forces behind the adaptive evolution of human proteins. By analysing human variation data we found that PSRs are enriched in benign but depleted in pathogenic substitutions, extending previous observations that positively selected genes contain elevated levels of missense variation. Notably, PSGs of the large-scale dataset were also enriched among clinical-stage drug targets, suggesting a potential link between positive selection and pharmacological relevance. Conclusion Together, our results provide a refined structural model of adaptive evolution in human proteins and identify extracellular exposed molecular recognition surfaces and human-pathogen interaction interfaces as recurrent hotspots of positive selection. Our results point to the direction that precise identification of human PSRs could delineate important host-pathogen interfaces that exert evolutionary selection pressure on humans and appoint novel targets with therapeutic potential.

research.abstract: Abstract The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M. tuberculosis ). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 Å, 3.51 Å, 3.70 Å and 3.22 Å, respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5–C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: DEG (Degradation of periplasmic proteins) proteases are ATP-independent serine endopeptidases found in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes including plants. They are considered to be key regulators of development and stress tolerance in plants. In this study, a comprehensive genome-wide analysis identified 19 serine protease-like DEG family proteins in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.), revealing their structural diversity, domain architecture, and regulatory potential. Physiochemical profiling showed a predominance of acidic isoelectric points (pI), variable protein lengths (169–1083 amino acids), and differential stability indices. Subcellular localization predicted most DEG proteases to reside in the chloroplast, with others distributed across cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisome. Domain analysis confirmed the universal presence of the trypsin domain, with varying numbers of PDZ domains and additional conserved motifs among paralogs. Evolutionary divergence analysis of StDEG genes and their orthologs from six Solanaceae species as well as Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa, and Zea mays revealed dN/dS ratios below one for all orthologous pairs, suggesting that StDEG genes have evolved under strong purifying selection and remained highly conserved throughout plant evolution. Gene ontology annotations linked DEG proteases to key biological functions including PSII repair, photoinhibition, and chloroplast organization, alongside protein catabolism and light stimulus response. Promoter analysis revealed an abundance of cis-regulatory elements (CREs), particularly light-responsive motifs, along with hormone and stress-related elements such as ABRE, ARE, and MBS. Expression profiling across eight developmental tissues demonstrated tissue-specific expression patterns, with strong transcript accumulation of selected DEG members in senescent leaf, stolon, shoot apex, and tuber. Interestingly, several splice variants showed unique expression dynamics, including stage-specific and stress-induced activation. Upon exposure to abiotic and hormonal cues, 16 DEG proteases displayed significant transcriptional modulation, particularly under light, ABA, and Zeatin treatments, with notable fold changes reaching up to 26-fold in certain variants. These findings highlight the functional versatility of DEG proteases in potato development and stress adaptation, especially their responsiveness to light and hormonal stimuli. The characterization of these proteases paves the way for future studies on their roles in crop resilience and genome editing applications.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding variation in molecular evolutionary rates among species offers insight into the forces shaping evolution, and can inform phylogenetic models and molecular dating. Explaining this variation is challenging, however. Analyses must account for phylogenetic relationships, correlated species traits, and features of substitution rate estimates that standard approaches like phylogenetic generalised least squares (PGLS) do not address. Notably, substitution rates describe change accumulated over time along the lineages of a phylogeny, where shorter branches have higher variance in substitution rate estimation. Traits like body mass, by contrast, are instantaneous measurements and are therefore properties of nodes or tips, rather than branches. Here, we formalise an approach that overcomes these problems using phylogenetic pairwise contrasts (PPC). By comparing differences between pairs of taxa, we avoid estimating traits at internal nodes. Pairs are sampled from a phylogeny so that the edges connecting them do not overlap with any other pairs, generating comparisons that can be analysed using a linear regression. Simulations show that PPC tolerates measurement error in both traits and substitution rates while keeping its false positive rate close to nominal. PGLS, by contrast, is poorly calibrated for finding covariates of substitution rate, with up to 35% of replicates yielding p < 0.01 when no true association exists. We “ground-truth” PPC using empirical datasets, corroborating the well-established negative correlation between body size and substitution rate in flowering plants and mammals. This work offers a straightforward, reliable method for linking substitution rates to biological traits, implemented in the R package phylowise.

research.abstract: Abstract Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on ‘attaching and effacing’ lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.

research.abstract: The family Noctuidae includes agricultural pests that vary in geographic distribution and host range. This study analyzed 30 mitogenomes representing 14 noctuid species; Ostrinia nubilalis (Crambidae) served as the phylogenetic outgroup. The genomes contained the typical complement of 37 mitochondrial genes and exhibited conserved gene order, pronounced A + T enrichment, and a preference for A/T-ending synonymous codons. A neutrality regression based on species means revealed a modest positive association between GC3 and GC12 (R 2 = 0.3201; p = 0.03494), although it could not distinguish the respective contributions of mutation and selection. Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian analyses of 13 protein-coding genes (11,229 bp) agreed on 26 of the 28 internal groupings in the maximum-likelihood tree, including a strongly supported Spodoptera clade. Differences in deeper relationships occurred at nodes with limited support. All 13 genes had dN/dS estimates below one (0.00306-0.01691), consistent with purifying selection. Codon usage varied among gene categories, and gene-wise codon bias was not significantly associated with dN/dS. Five crop-associated species with multiple larval host plants and documented long-distance migration- Helicoverpa armigera, Athetis lepigone, Spodoptera litura, S. frugiperda, and Mamestra brassicae -fell below the fitted neutrality regression line. Whether their ecological traits relate to this pattern remains requires broader taxonomic sampling and ecological data in future investigations.

research.abstract: The GRAS gene family, a plant-specific family of transcription factors, plays critical roles in diverse developmental processes and abiotic stress responses. Although extensive studies on the identification and functional characterization of GRAS genes have been conducted in numerous plant species, systematic analyses of this family in Salvia miltiorrhiza, a valuable traditional Chinese medicinal herb, remain limited. The present study aims to identify and characterize GRAS genes in S. miltiorrhiza, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of their phylogenetic evolution, functional divergence, and tissue-specific expression profiles​. In this study, a total of 33 GRAS genes were identified in S. miltiorrhiza and subjected to comprehensive analysis. Phylogenetic analysis classified these genes into eight distinct subgroups and identified eight pairs of paralogs. Genetic divergence analysis revealed that the GRAS gene family has predominantly undergone purifying selection, as evidenced by Ka/Ks ratios below 1 for all eight paralogous pairs. Positive selection analysis using the site and branch-site models further suggested that SmGRAS genes had gone through purifying selective pressure for adaptive evolution. Motif analysis showed that group-specific motifs likely contribute to functional divergence among subgroups. Functional divergence analysis suggested that subgroup-specific genes may have experienced functional divergence during evolution, and provided preliminary insights into the molecular mechanisms potentially underlying their divergent functions. Tissue-specific expression analysis revealed that SmGRAS genes might perform distinct functions in different tissues. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the GRAS gene family in S. miltiorrhiza. Taken together, these results elucidate a comprehensive understanding of the GRAS gene family and furnish robust references for subsequent functional investigations of GRAS genes in S. miltiorrhiza.

research.abstract: Zoonotic tuberculosis (zTB), caused by animal-adapted members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), is classically attributed to M. bovis but is increasingly linked to M. orygis across South Asia. Species-level MTBC identification is rarely performed in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), leaving the zTB burden poorly defined. Bangladesh has endemic bovine tuberculosis, a growing dairy sector, unpasteurised-milk consumption, and expanding captive wildlife collections, yet the evidence has not been synthesised by diagnostic reliability. This systematic evidence map aimed to collate the evidence on zTB in Bangladesh and to review the diagnostic methods used to identify animal-adapted MTBC species, particularly M. bovis and M. orygis , in livestock, wildlife, and humans. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and BanglaJOL from the 1970s to June 2026; CAB Abstracts, Scopus, and Web of Science were not accessible. Two reviewers independently screened and appraised studies using the JBI checklist, assigning each to a five-level diagnostic evidence hierarchy (Level 1: WGS, phylogeny, RD typing, spoligotyping, or MLVA; Level 5: tuberculin skin test or serology only). These non-comparable tests precluded meta-analysis; therefore, findings are presented as an evidence map. Thirty-five studies met the inclusion criteria: 24 on prevalence in cattle/buffaloes, 10 on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in cattle, captive wildlife, and humans, and 1 specifically on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in humans. Most livestock studies used non-discriminatory tests (tuberculin skin tests, ELISA, or untyped PCR) and reported non-comparable reactor proportions of 1.2% to 33.7%. The few studies using species-level methods (Levels 1–2) confirmed M. orygis in cattle and in at least seven captive wildlife species, including monkeys, using marker-based molecular assays. Several historical reports of M. bovis were based on non-discriminatory PCR or serology, which cannot reliably distinguish among MTBC members. Human evidence was limited to three studies, including one WGS-confirmed M. orygis case identified through tuberculosis surveillance. In published reports from Bangladesh, M. orygis is the only animal-adapted MTBC member molecularly confirmed at the cattle–wildlife–human interface; existing M. bovis claims lack discriminatory support and require cautious reinterpretation. zTB surveillance should therefore move beyond an M. bovis -only framework and integrate species-level MTBC identification into a staged, resource-appropriate One Health strategy across animal, wildlife, and human health.

research.abstract: Background Members of the Triatoma brasiliensis species complex are among the primary vectors of Chagas disease in northeastern Brazil. Despite their epidemiological importance, mitogenomic resources for this group remain limited, constraining comparative and evolutionary analyses at the genomic scale. Methods We assembled and annotated twelve near-complete mitochondrial genomes representing four taxa of the T. brasiliensis complex ( T. b. brasiliensis , T. melanica , T. sherlocki , and T. petrocchiae ), with three specimens per taxon. Genome annotation and gene-specific analyses were conducted to assess patterns of sequence and structural variation across taxa. A concatenated dataset including protein-coding genes, rRNAs, and tRNAs was analyzed under a partitioned maximum likelihood framework, with partitions defined by gene and codon position. Results All mitogenomes exhibited the canonical insect gene complement and gene order. Genome length variation (16,277–17,238 bp) involved variation in non-coding regions, including the A + T-rich control region and an expanded intergenic spacer between tRNA-Ser(UCN) and ND1 in T. petrocchiae, driven by tandem repeats. Among protein-coding genes, ND6 showed the highest nucleotide variability and elevated amino-acid variability relative to most other mitochondrial genes, with structural differences among the examined taxa. Phylogenetic analyses recovered the sampled members of the T. brasiliensis species complex as a fully supported monophyletic clade. Conclusion The marked variation observed in ND6, including distinct amino-acid motifs among the examined specimens, suggests that this gene may contain potentially informative variation for lineage-level evolutionary studies. However, the restricted geographic sampling, the limited number of specimens per taxon, and the incomplete representation of the T. brasiliensis complex constrain the generalizability of these findings. Broader geographic and taxonomic sampling will be required to determine the consistency and taxonomic significance of these patterns, while the mitogenomic dataset as a whole expands the resources available for investigating mitochondrial diversity and evolutionary relationships in Triatominae.

research.abstract: The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli , the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae , in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli , strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sputum culture conversion in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is the most important interim indicator for drug-resistant (DR) tuberculosis (TB) treatment effectiveness. Bedaquiline-based regimens offer the possibility of more effective and less toxic treatment for DR TB. Bedaquiline-based regimens have been adopted as the new standard of care for DR TB, replacing the oto-and nephrotoxic aminoglycosides. We determined the median time to sputum culture conversion (TTCC) and associated factors among RR and MDR TB patients treated with Bedaquiline-based regimens, at Mulago National Referral Hospital, Uganda. METHODS: In a longitudinal type of observational study performed at Mulago Hospital, between January 2020 and June 2023, RR and MDR TB patients' records were reviewed to obtain data on socio-demographic and clinical factors, and TTCC. The study outcome was TTCC, recorded as time from RR/MDR TB treatment initiation to sputum culture conversion, which was defined as at least 2 consecutive negative TB sputum cultures, at least 30 days apart, for a RR/MDR PTB patient who was sputum culture positive at baseline. Analysis for median TTCC was done using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and the log-logistic parametric survival regression model was used to identify predictors for TTCC. RESULTS: Of the 265 participants, 196 (74.0%) were male, with median age of 35(IQR:27-42) years. The median TTCC was 7 (IQR:4-8) weeks from treatment initiation. Grade 2 + baseline smear positivity (adjusted Time Ratio (aTR):1.24, 95% CI:1.02-1.51, p = 0.029), grade 3 + baseline smear positivity (aTR:1.62, 95% CI:1.30-2.01, p < 0.001), cavitary disease on CXR (aTR:1.36, 95% CI:1.18-1.56, p < 0.001), and pleural effusion on CXR (aTR:1.81, 95% CI:1.43-2.31, p < 0.001) significantly prolonged the TTCC. Diabetes mellitus (7/265) significantly reduced the TTCC (aTR: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.22 - 0.60, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The WHO long regimen (9 months) was indistinguishable from the shorter 6-months regimen for the time to culture conversion. Integration of TB screening at points of care of high-risk patients like diabetics remains important for early detection and prompt initiation of DR TB treatment for better outcomes. The TB program and clinicians should enhance and individualize support for RR/MDR TB patients with more severe disease, to ensure optimum TTCC and successful treatment outcomes. research.abstract: BACKGROUND: India, the capital of tuberculosis (TB) worldwide, accounts for 27% of the global burden of drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). Managing DR-TB in itself is challenging, and preexisting multiorgan dysfunction makes it even more lengthy and complex. Here, we share our real-world experience in successfully managing a difficult-to-treat case of rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), a type of DR-TB, in a high-risk patient with multiple comorbidities. CASE PRESENTATION: A 60-year-old 70 kg male diagnosed with RR-TB was referred from a District DR-TB Centre to our Nodal DR-TB Centre for pretreatment evaluation and treatment initiation in December 2022. Baseline evaluation revealed severe renal dysfunction, hepatic dysfunction, a prolonged QT interval, and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, necessitating an individualized all-oral longer regimen with appropriate dose adjustments guided by the National Programmatic Management of Drug-resistant Tuberculosis Guidelines. During treatment, the regimen was sequentially individualized in response to evolving suspected adverse drug reactions, with each modification aimed at optimizing patient safety while maintaining an effective treatment regimen. The patient showed radiological improvement, achieved sputum culture conversion, and successfully completed the 18-month treatment by June 2024. The patient did not relapse during the 18-month follow-up period (December 2025). CONCLUSION: This case report exemplifies the success of personalized pharmacotherapeutic decision-making in challenging cases. Structured toxicity assessment and intensive clinical, laboratory, and electrocardiography monitoring in addition to timely treatment modification may facilitate successful treatment in carefully selected high-risk RR-TB patients when standard regimens are not feasible, even in resource-limited settings. research.abstract: Abstract Darwinian evolution has produced two types of functional polymers with different chemical alphabets, RNA and proteins. Dominance of proteins across many cellular functions in extant organisms has been classically attributed to catalytic superiority over RNA. From this perspective, functional RNAs are fossils from the origin of life, where they possibly kick-started molecular evolution. Yet, in addition to direct catalytic capability, the chemical alphabets of RNA and proteins give rise to distinct evolving codes. A crucial question is therefore how the evolution of functional structures is shaped by mutational variation for each of these codes. Here, we employ RNAfold and ESMFold structure predictions to directly compare mutational profiles— i.e . the distribution of secondary structures upon point mutations—of functional RNA and proteins. Unlike RNA, natural protein structures feature a narrow mutational profile with high mutational robustness but limited structural variation. Moreover, while functional and random RNA sequences share similar mutational profiles, secondary structures of natural proteins are substantially more robust than those of random sequences and de novo proteins, revealing an evolutionary drive toward robustness. Integrating structure prediction with phylogenetic data and simulations, we find evidence for the hypothesis that robust protein structures are favored by selection to buffer errors in translation. As a side-effect, the propensity for structural innovation is reduced in proteins. Our results show that protein folds have evolutionary properties distinct from RNA structures, with implications for the origin of function in both types of molecules—in present-day organisms, as well as during the origin of life. Significance statement How changes in RNA and protein sequences propagate to their structure through the folding process is fundamental to understanding the evolutionary behavior and functional potential of these polymers. Using computational structure predictions, we argue that protein structures have been selected to exhibit high robustness to translation errors, which, as a side-effect, limits access to structural variants for evolutionary innovation. In stark contrast, RNA structures are innately robust and evolvable, and show no signature of selection. Our work thus shows how mutational effects can be molded by evolution for fixed genotype-phenotype maps. In maps that themselves evolve, such as gene regulatory networks, the imprint of past selection is likely even stronger.

research.abstract: Abstract The Wnt gene family plays a central role in vertebrate development, yet its evolutionary dynamics across lineages remain largely unexplored. Here, we present the most comprehensive analysis of Wnt gene evolution in vertebrates to date, leveraging a large-scale comparative genomics approach of 38,886 Wnt gene sequences mined from 1,961 species. We first investigate overall patterns of gene retention, duplication, and loss, and then focus specifically on the impact of whole-genome duplications (WGDs). We uncover striking variation in Wnt gene repertoire sizes, with ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) exhibiting the largest repertoires – even after excluding taxa with recent WGDs. Notably, we identify extreme expansions in polyploid cyprinids, including an octoploid hybrid harbouring 99 Wnt genes, the highest number observed. Unexpectedly elevated Wnt copy numbers in diploid species, such as in the Antarctic lanternfish (Electrona antarctica) and the brook lamprey (Lethenteron reissneri), point to lineage-specific expansions, although the potential adaptive significance of these expansions remains to be tested. Evolutionary rate analyses reveal that certain Wnt clades – especially Wnt8 and Wnt16 – exhibit elevated dN/dS ratios and high birth–death rates, consistent with repeated episodes of relaxed constraint and/or adaptive diversification. Contrary to our expectations, there was no relationship between developmental expression timing and evolutionary rates, suggesting pleiotropic regulation and functional redundancy of Wnt genes. Altogether, our findings reveal widespread variation in Wnt copy number and turnover among lineages, shaped by both genome duplication history and divergent evolutionary trajectories. This work provides a high-resolution framework for understanding the molecular evolution of a key developmental toolkit and highlights candidate genes for future studies of vertebrate eco-morphological diversity.

research.abstract: Background: Takotsubo syndrome, which predominantly affects women, is thought to be precipitated by catecholamine excess, yet unstable patients often receive intravenous inotropes. We examined the association between intravenous inotropes and 30-day mortality in a nationwide cohort. Methods: We identified all patients with a first angiographic diagnosis of Takotsubo syndrome in the Swedish Coronary Angiography and Angioplasty Registry from 2008 through August 2025, linked to coronary care and population registers. The primary analysis was a Cox model for 30-day death among patients with a coronary care record, adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and Killip class, with multiple imputation. Sensitivity analyses varied the covariates and standard errors and examined days 0 to 7 and 8 to 30 separately, and the association was estimated in women and men with an interaction term. Results: Of 3,458 patients (79.4% women), 141 (4.1%) received inotropes: 3.6% of women and 5.8% of men. Thirty-day mortality was 19.9% in treated and 1.7% in untreated patients. The unadjusted hazard ratio was 12.89 (95% CI, 8.20 to 20.26) and the adjusted hazard ratio 6.49 (3.49 to 12.08; P<0.001; E-value, 12.5). In sensitivity analyses, the hazard ratio ranged from 3.37 (1.88 to 6.03), with presenting symptom and laboratory values added, to 6.62 (3.63 to 12.08). The hazard ratio was 8.82 (4.47 to 17.39) for days 0 to 7 and 2.47 (0.65 to 9.36) for days 8 to 30, and 6.43 (3.15 to 13.16) in women and 6.59 (2.79 to 15.58) in men (P=0.96 for interaction). Conclusions: Intravenous inotropes were associated with higher 30-day mortality in Takotsubo syndrome, in both women and men, with most of the excess in the first week.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future. METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods. RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis. DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers. CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

research.abstract: Detecting signatures of positive selection in genomes is a common application of population genetics and one of the most influential models for this task is the hard selective sweep where a de novo mutation rapidly fixes. Many statistics aim to detect hard sweeps by summarizing signatures left behind in the site frequency spectrum, linkage disequilibrium, and haplotype frequencies. However, potentially undiscovered signals could still exist. We attempted to test whether any undiscovered signatures of hard sweeps exist by comparing a convolutional neural network, which can learn signatures from raw data without any prior knowledge, to known summary sweep statistics for inferring the time to fixation ( t f ) of a hard sweep in a background of variable sweep ages ( t a ). Across approximately 250,000 simulations encompassing 5 different demographic scenarios of single panmictic populations, a convolutional neural network model trained directly on raw genotype data failed to better predict t f than methods based purely on common summary statistics. This suggests that few undiscovered signals remain in single timepoint, single population genotype data to better predict t f . However, future models can explore additional demographic spaces and penalize use of known population genetic features to potentially improve this search.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches—including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks—have substantially expanded the chemical space accessible for early-stage anti-TB research. However, their translational success remains limited. This discrepancy reflects a fundamental mismatch between target-centric computational paradigms and the multi-scale biological constraints of Mtb , including permeability barriers, efflux mechanisms, metabolic state heterogeneity, lesion-level pharmacokinetics, and regimen-dependent therapeutic effects. This review critically evaluates current computational strategies for anti-TB drug screening, with particular emphasis on their performance under TB-specific biological and resistance constraints. We further explore computational approaches designed to address drug-resistant Mtb , including resistance-aware compound design, host-directed therapy, and combination regimen modeling. Finally, we explore key limitations in current computational pipelines, including challenges in data quality, biological integration, and regimen-level modeling, and propose a shift toward biologically grounded, regimen-aware, and systems-level frameworks. Bridging the gap between in silico prediction and clinical efficacy will require integrating multi-scale biological realism into computational pipelines, enabling more reliable translation of computational advances into effective anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: Abstract The basic leucine zipper ATF-like transcription factor (BATF) plays a pivotal role in coordinating various aspects of lymphoid cell biology, yet essential functions in plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) have not been reported. Here, we demonstrate that BATF deficiency leads to increased interferon (IFN) I production in Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)-activated pDCs, while BATF overexpression has an inhibitory effect. BATF-deficient mice exhibit elevated IFN-I serum levels early in lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection. Integrated transcriptomics and ChIP-seq approaches identified the transcriptional regulator DC-SCRIPT as a direct target of BATF that suppresses IFN-I promoter activity by interacting with interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7). Genome-wide association study (GWAS) analyses further implicate BATF in pDC-mediated human diseases. Our findings establish a novel negative feedback axis in IFN-I regulation in pDCs during antiviral immune responses orchestrated by BATF and DC-SCRIPT, with broader implications for pDC- and IFN-I-mediated autoimmunity. Significance Statement Type I interferons (IFN-I) are essential for antiviral immunity but, when dysregulated, can promote inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) are specialized producers of IFN-I, yet the mechanisms that prevent excessive IFN-I production remain incompletely understood. We identify the transcription factor BATF as a negative regulator of IFN-I production in pDCs and uncover a BATF-DC-SCRIPT regulatory axis that restrains this response. Following TLR activation, BATF directly induces DC-SCRIPT by binding its regulatory regions. DC-SCRIPT then interacts with the key IFN-I transcription factor IRF7 to limit IFN-I gene expression. Thus, BATF and DC-SCRIPT control a negative-feedback mechanism that modulates the magnitude and duration of pDC-mediated IFN-I responses, providing a framework for understanding and potentially therapeutically modulating IFN-I-driven inflammation.

research.abstract: Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a common complication of diabetes, and in Bangladesh laboratory testing for it is not always available. Questionnaire answers could help decide whom to test first, but small machine-learning studies often report optimistic accuracy. Methods We analysed a public dataset of 400 adults with at least 10 years of diabetes attending a tertiary hospital in Dhaka, 185 with a hospital diagnosis of CKD. A pre-specified ridge logistic regression using 20 non-invasive features was developed and internally validated with nested cross-validation (five folds, ten repeats), compared with lasso, random forest and gradient boosting, and assessed for discrimination, calibration and net benefit. Simulations examined case-enriched sampling and single train/test splits. Results The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.75 (95% confidence interval 0.70-0.80; optimism-corrected 0.76). Flexible algorithms were not detectably better (differences -0.005 to +0.006). Calibration within the sample was good (slope 1.06, 0.79-1.33), and testing the highest-scoring 30% of patients would have found 48% of CKD cases. The sample was smaller than the 883 patients recommended. Urinary infection, body-mass index, insulin use, diabetes duration and pain-killer use were positively associated with CKD and diet adherence negatively; regular walking and hypertension showed directions opposite to clinical expectation, consistent with features recorded after diagnosis. The yearly history added no reliable information. In simulation, case-enriched sampling preserved the AUC but overstated absolute risk (mean predicted risk 0.37 at a true prevalence of 0.10). Over 300 random 80/20 splits of the same data, the test AUC ranged from 0.61 to 0.87; reporting the best of ten splits would overstate it by about 0.07. Conclusions Questionnaire features moderately distinguished patients with an existing CKD diagnosis. Whether they identify patients before diagnosis requires external validation in patients assessed before CKD status is known. The study was not registered.

research.abstract: Background Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors reduce cardiovascular and kidney events in adults with type 2 diabetes(T2DM) and cardiorenal disease, but treatment initiation among eligible patients remains incompletely characterized. We estimated the cumulative incidence of recorded SGLT2 inhibitor initiation and associated participant characteristics in a diverse U.S. cohort. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study leveraging electronic health record data from the All of Us Research Program. Adults with confirmed type 2 diabetes, at least one co-occurring cardiorenal condition (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease), and no prior SGLT2 inhibitor use were followed from the earliest date all criteria were met during 2019-2023. The 365-day cumulative incidence of initiation was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method, accounting for competing risk of all-cause mortality. Cause-specific modified Poisson regression with robust error variance yielded adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) for initiation predictors Results Among 9,333 eligible participants, 637 had recorded SGLT2 inhibitor initiation within 365 days (estimated cumulative incidence, 6.85% (95% CI 6.34-7.36)). The 365-day incidence was 8.40% among individuals with heart failure, 6.65% with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and 5.28% with chronic kidney disease. Initiation was more likely with heart failure (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.29-1.76), and glycated hemoglobin [≥]9.0% versus <7.0% (RR 2.61, 95% CI 2.07-3.28), but less likely with chronic kidney disease (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.54-0.74), age [≥]75 versus 45-64 years (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.40-0.65), and non-Hispanic Black versus non-Hispanic White race and ethnicity (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.97). Conclusions Fewer than 1 in 10 eligible, untreated adults with T2D and cardiorenal disease initiated SGLT2 inhibitor therapy within one year. Even with expanding guideline indications, substantial implementation gaps persist, particularly among patients with CKD, older adults, and non-Hispanic Black adults. Targeted health systems are imperative to optimize the use of guideline-recommended cardiorenal therapies.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: H14 avian influenza viruses (AIVs) are rare, with limited data on their circulation in mainland China. This study investigated the ecological origins and zoonotic potential of H14 viruses in southern China. The isolates were characterised by full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis, together with assessment of avian- and human-type receptor binding, in vitro replication in avian, mammalian, and human cell lines, and in vivo pathogenicity in mice. Four H14 AIVs (one H14N6, two H14N7, and one H14N8) were isolated. We identified a novel H14 transmission network involving Mareca penelope and various shorebird species, indicating a multihost dispersal mechanism. Guangdong isolates formed a distinct subclade within the Eurasian lineage, closely related to Russian and Cambodian strains. The isolates (SZ3742/H14N6, ZJ3523/H14N7, SZ3536/H14N8) exhibited dual receptor-binding specificity for avian (α-2,3) and human (α-2,6) sialic acids. Strain-dependent replication in human A549 cells showed SZ3742/H14N6 peaked comparably to DF-1 cells but lower than MDCK cells, while the others had lower peak titres. All isolates replicated transiently at low titres in mouse lungs with limited pathogenicity. Molecular characterisation revealed mammalian adaptation markers and a typical HA cleavage site motif (PDKQTR↓GLF). This study presents the first evidence of H14 AIV circulation in Guangdong, emphasising the need for enhanced surveillance in the East Asian -Australasian Flyway.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an increasingly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition with multifactorial origins, including potential prenatal environmental contributions. Maternal anemia (decreased hemoglobin [Hb] levels) has long been associated with adverse offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes, yet evidence regarding elevated levels of antenatal hemoglobin levels, in relation to ASD risk remains limited. This study evaluated the association between maternal Hb levels during pregnancy and the risk of ASD diagnosis in offspring. Methods This large-scale, population-based retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from births of members of Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, between 2011 and 2021. The study included 303,234 singleton live births to Jewish mothers who had at least one measured prenatal Hb value and were CHS members. Exclusion criteria were children with known genetic disorders and births <25 weeks of gestation. Maternal Hb, and red blood cells (RBC) levels during the first and second trimesters were categorized as low (<2.5th percentile), normal (reference), or high (>97.5th percentile). The main outcome was a diagnosis of ASD in the offspring, as recorded in medical files. Statistical analyses adjusted for maternal age, socioeconomic status, gestational diabetes, BMI, and other clinical and demographic factors. Results Among the 303,234 births, 8,106 (2.7%) children were diagnosed with ASD. High maternal Hb levels were associated with elevated odds of ASD diagnosis (aOR=1.22; 95% CI=1.08-1.37), with the strongest association observed for first-trimester measurements (aOR=1.31; 95% CI=1.14-1.49). This association persisted in the sibling-matched analysis (aOR=1.64; 95% CI=1.08–2.47) and was not modified by maternal RBC levels, suggesting that it was not explained by familial factors or RBC counts. The main limitations of this study include the lack of available data on maternal smoking, and the absence of detailed information on maternal nutritional status. Conclusions These findings suggest that elevated antenatal Hb levels may be relevant to offspring neurodevelopment. Further studies are needed to replicate these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying this association.

research.abstract: Abstract A vast degree of phenotypic variation can be seen across lineages of eukaryotes. Although at least part of this diversity has a genomic basis, it is unclear whether there are broad-scale links that can be detected between rates of genomic and phenotypic evolution. The presence of a correlation would imply the action of shared drivers, such as mutational or adaptive processes that occur on a genome- and organism-wide scale. We investigated this question by using a phylogenetic approach to test for correlations between molecular and morphological evolutionary rates. We analysed 60 data sets of combined nucleotide sequences and discrete morphological characters, representing a diverse range of eukaryotes. Using a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic approach based on sister-pair contrasts, we found very little evidence of any link between rates of molecular and morphological evolution, a striking result given the scale and taxonomic breadth of our analyses. Our results point to contrasting evolutionary dynamics underlying genomes and phenotypic traits; these have led to greater variation in morphological evolutionary rates across lineages, whereas molecular evolution is more clocklike. Our study reveals the discrepancies in evolutionary drivers that act at the genomic and phenotypic levels across the eukaryotic Tree of Life.

research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

One DRH-1 orthologue from each of 11 Caenorhabditis species was curated from WormBase ParaSite release 19 under explicit orthology and sequence-quality rules. Codon alignments from MAFFT, PRANK and BABAPPAlign, with trimming and taxon-deletion sensitivities, were analysed with HyPhy (BUSTED, aBSREL, MEME, RELAX, GARD) and PAML codeml. Single-hit codon models supported episodic diversification on the lineage ancestral to C. panamensis and C. waitukubuli. Jointly modelling synonymous rate variation and multinucleotide substitutions improved the BUSTED fit by 76.25 AICc units and removed gene-wide significance; focal aBSREL and RELAX results also became nonsignificant. Ancestral reconstruction retained an H370L change, which was examined on the RNA-bound DRH-1 structure (PDB 8T5S) with local Rosetta calculations.

research.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and glaucoma are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet whether external eye photographs carry phenotypic information about posterior segment disease remains unclear, and methods to mitigate demographic disparities in such models are largely unexplored. We developed and evaluated deep learning and vision-language models for binary classification of vision-threatening DR (VTDR), advanced AMD, and glaucoma using 40,687 external eye photographs from 9,878 patients at Massachusetts Eye and Ear. Convolutional networks (WResNet, EfficientNet), a vision transformer (ViT), and a finetuned vision-language model (LLaVA) were assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with fairness across sex, race, and ethnicity quantified by the equity-scaled AUC (ES-AUC). Five fairness-training strategies were applied to the best models. LLaVA achieved the highest baseline AUC for VTDR (85{middle dot}4%, comparable to ViT 82{middle dot}6%); advanced AMD was similar across architectures (EfficientNet 86{middle dot}3%; LLaVA 84{middle dot}8%; ViT 84{middle dot}7%), whereas glaucoma was substantially worse (67-74%). Fairness training improved VTDR and AMD AUCs to 86{middle dot}3% and 85{middle dot}9% while partially mitigating demographic disparities. In summary, although AI models that rely on external eye photography to detect posterior segment disease may not yet be suitable for clinical deployment, the fairness methods demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study could be applied to other AI systems to decrease performance disparities and potentially improve model performance.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT The leech gut is known to be a viral reservoir, where viruses can persist long-term and are protected from external influences. Therefore, leeches can serve as vectors for transmission of viral disease to susceptible hosts on which they prey. Nonetheless, viral diversity and virus-leech-host interactions remain largely unknown, with hitherto no research directed at identifying viruses that use leeches as their hosts. In the present study, we report the discovery of a novel large DNA virus (phylum Nucleocytoviricota ) recovered from genomic sequencing data of the common fish leech Piscicola geometra (Linnaeus, 1761). Through genomic and phylogenetic analyses, we identify this lineage as highly divergent from currently known viruses, with ~95% of its predicted protein-coding genes showing no identifiable homology with current databases. Whether the leech is a host of this virus or a vector that transmits it to fish species remains to be investigated. This work highlights the value of off-target sequence retrieval for discovering novel viral lineages and sets the stage for future studies directed towards the prevalence and biology of leech-associated large DNA viruses.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Individuals of African genetic ancestry are at high risk for heart failure (HF), which is often preceded by cardiac structural and functional abnormalities. Nevertheless, little is known about cardiac structure and function among Afro-Caribbeans residing in Tobago. This study aimed to investigate the epidemiology of cardiac structure and function among African Caribbeans in Tobago. Methods A total of 924 participants (41-83 years) underwent clinical evaluation and transthoracic echocardiography. Images were analyzed for left ventricular (LV) mass index (MI), left atrial volume index, diastolic dysfunction (DD), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e′ ratio, E/A ratio, and other echocardiographic measures. Cardiac structure and function were evaluated by age, sex, and HF stage. Results The mean age was 61.7 years, with 61.4% women, 47.8% obesity, and 20.2% diabetes. Average systolic blood pressure was approximately 140 mmHg, and 76.7% had hypertension. Abnormal LV geometry was present in 77.1% of participants, predominantly concentric remodeling (69.5%). The prevalence of DD was 13.4%, LVEF <50% was 1.5%, and abnormal GLS (≤-18%) was 5.2%. Women had significantly higher E/e′ ratios and a higher prevalence of Stage A and Stage B HF, whereas men had a higher prevalence of symptomatic (Stage C) HF. Participants aged 65-83 years had significantly higher E/e′ ratio, concentric remodeling, and LV hypertrophy than those aged 41-57 years. Conclusions Women and older adults have higher LV structural abnormalities and DD than men and younger adults. These results will be helpful to inform public health priorities related to cardiovascular health in Tobago.
