research.abstract: BACKGROUND: People with the same number of unresolved cardiometabolic problems may be at different stages of care. Whether care stage provides information on subsequent cardiovascular risk beyond the number of unresolved problems remains unclear. METHODS: We analyzed longitudinal data from CHARLS, HRS, and ELSA. Measurements, diagnoses, and treatment information were used to classify care states at each landmark. Cohort-specific adjusted Cox models estimated associations with subsequent cardiovascular disease (CVD), heart disease, and stroke. We tested whether stage added information beyond gap count and whether count remained informative after stage was considered. We also directly compared blood pressure, glycemic, and lipid targets within the same stage. RESULTS: CHARLS included 7,899 participants. HRS and ELSA included 20,531 and 12,071 landmark observations from 12,933 and 6,491 participants, respectively. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for CVD per additional gap were 1.31 (1.23-1.41), 1.18 (1.13-1.23), and 1.09 (1.03-1.16). With exactly 1 gap, HRs for treated but uncontrolled (TA) versus unrecognized (U) gaps were 2.09 (1.70-2.57), 1.34 (1.19-1.51), and 1.27 (1.07-1.50) after adjustment for the affected target. Single-gap care stage provided additional information on CVD and heart disease risk beyond gap count in all 3 cohorts. Outcomes also differed between 2 and 3 gaps after accounting for stage in CHARLS and HRS. Under cohort-specific definitions, TA was the most common glycemic gap stage in all 3 cohorts, whereas U predominated among lipid gaps in CHARLS and ELSA. CVD associations were stronger for unrecognized glycemic gaps than for unrecognized blood pressure or lipid gaps in CHARLS. At the TA stage in HRS, associations were stronger for blood pressure and glycemic gaps than for lipid gaps. CONCLUSIONS: Gap count and care stage provide complementary prognostic information. The count-stage framework first records how many cardiometabolic targets remain unresolved, then identifies each affected target and its care stage to describe where further assessment is needed. research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: Introduction Abutilon fruticosum Guill. & Perr. is a drought-tolerant Malvaceae subshrub native to Saudi Arabia. However, no mitochondrial genome has previously been reported for the genus Abutilon . This study reports the first complete mitochondrial genome of A. fruticosum and evaluates its comparative and phylogenetic relationships within Malvaceae. Methods The mitochondrial genome was assembled, annotated, and analyzed for genome composition, repetitive sequences, codon usage, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitution rates, collinearity, and phylogenetic relationships inferred from 32 shared mitochondrial protein-coding genes across ten taxa. Results The mitogenome was assembled as a circular molecule of 826,313 bp, with a GC content of 44.94%, and contained 37 protein-coding genes, 3 rRNA genes, and 21 tRNA genes. Comparative analyses of five Malvaceae mitogenomes revealed conserved codon-usage patterns, with weak-to-moderate bias influenced by nucleotide composition and functional constraints, but substantial variation in repeat abundance and distribution. DeepredMT predicted 397 RNA-editing sites in A. fruticosum , fewer than in Tilia amurensis , Gossypium trilobum , and Hibiscus cannabinus , but slightly more than in Adansonia perrieri . Simple sequence repeats and short dispersed repeats predominated, whereas G. trilobum had the greatest proportion of long repeats and H. cannabinus the highest repeat density. Nucleotide-diversity hotspots were detected in rpl16 , rps3 , cox2 , and rpl2 , while most protein-coding genes had dN/dS values below 1. The elevated dN/dS signal in rps4 suggested accelerated evolution or relaxed functional constraint, warranting further investigation. Maximum-likelihood analysis recovered A. fruticosum (tribe Malveae) as sister to the sampled Hibiscus – Gossypium clade with strong support. Discussion This study presents the first mitochondrial genome of Abutilon , expanding mitogenomic resources for Malvaceae. The A. fruticosum mitogenome shows conserved gene content and codon usage, alongside lineage-specific variation in repeat organization, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, and localized sequence divergence. The phylogenetic placement is consistent with the accepted classification of A. fruticosum in Malvoideae and illustrates the potential of mitogenomic data for systematic studies within Malvaceae, although broader taxon sampling is needed to test this placement. This mitogenome provides a resource for marker development, population-genetic studies, comparative mitogenomics, and phylogenetic research on Abutilon and related Malvaceae lineages.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) poses significant threats to animal health, public health, and wildlife conservation. Mycobacterium orygis, an emerging MTBC member, remains poorly characterized with respect to its epidemiology and transmission dynamics among Indian wildlife and livestock. METHODS: Fifty-five necropsy tissue samples from 21 captive wild animals were subjected to mycobacterial culture and a panel of molecular diagnostic assays, including multiplex PCR, Xpert-Ultra, and Truenat MTB/Rif. Confirmed MTBC isolates were characterized by drug susceptibility testing (GenoType MTBDRplus) and spoligotyping. Six isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and phylogenetic analyses were performed against publicly available reference genomes. RESULTS: Of 55 samples, 38 were MTBC-positive and 6 yielded nontuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility profiling revealed 28 pan-susceptible isolates, nine with isoniazid monoresistance, and one with rifampicin monoresistance. Spoligotyping classified 10 isolates as CAS1-Delhi, 27 as orphan lineages, and one remained unassigned. WGS of six isolates, representing diverse host species and tissue types, identified four as M. tuberculosis (CAS1-Delhi lineage). Notably, one orphan isolate from a blackbuck was reclassified as M. orygis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that this M. orygis strain was genetically distinct from other Indian wildlife strains and most closely related to a human-derived isolate from Karnataka, suggesting cross-host genomic relatedness. The remaining isolates clustered with Indian and global reference genomes; one was closely related to cattle-derived strains, whereas four were more closely related to human-derived strains. Low pairwise SNP distances (0-78 SNPs) with strong bootstrap support indicated close genomic relatedness across host species and geographic regions. CONCLUSION: This study shows the MTBC genomic diversity among various hosts. The phylogenetic relationships suggest that there is genetic relatedness among host populations such as M. orygis in a captive Indian blackbuck, which was in human contact for a long time. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance of mycobacterial infections at the human-animal interface and calls for more extensive, epidemiologically linked studies to look for cross-host transmission pathways.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how species diversity originates, accumulates and is sustained across heterogeneous regions is a core goal of macroevolutionary and conservation biology. The genus Huperzia is an ancient and cosmopolitan lineage of lycophytes, with species widely distributed in both temperate alpine and subtropical low‐ to mid‐elevation areas, offering ideal material for investigating the diversification history of early vascular plant lineages. Here, we utilized 87 plastid genomes from 23 species to reconstruct a robust phylogenetic framework within Huperzia and found that the development of the petiole and midrib should be considered supplementary diagnostic characters in future taxonomic revisions. Our spatiotemporal and spatial phylogenetic analyses indicated that temperate and montane regions, especially northeastern China and parts of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, preserve phylogenetically distinctive paleo‐lineages, whereas subtropical evergreen broad‐leaved forests contain younger lineages associated with ecological expansion and trait differentiation. This niche transition was accompanied by repeated leaf‐trait differentiation and shifts in plastid‐gene selection in subtropical lineages, with three positively selected genes ( rps19 , chlB and atpH ) identified by branch‐site analyses. This evolutionary strategy provides a new perspective for understanding how early vascular plants maintained a dynamic equilibrium between refugial conservatism and adaptive innovation.

research.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) combined with deep learning can detect metabolic signatures for classification of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). DesignCross-sectional analysis of participants included in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with FLIO imaging. Subjects1,783 participants from the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with HbA1c measurements and FLIO imaging scans: 425 normoglycemic, 569 prediabetic, and 789 diabetic. MethodsGlycemic groups were defined from self-reported diagnosis, glucose-lowering medication, and HbA1c. Center-of-mass mean lifetime ({tau}CMM) maps, corrected for background and system timing offset, were generated from the raw time-resolved FLIO scans. Group differences in central-window {tau}CMM were tested by one-way ANOVA and by age-adjusted analysis of covariance. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet-18, and XGBoost were trained on {tau}CMM maps for three-class (normal, prediabetic, diabetic) and two binary (normal vs. impaired; normal vs. diabetic) classification of T2DM and compared them with an age-only classifier and with models combining FLIO and age. Main Outcome MeasuresMacro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score, and positive predictive value (PPV). ResultsGroup-averaged {tau}CMM was longer in prediabetic and diabetic than in normoglycemic participants in both the SSC (p < 0.001) and the LSC (p < 0.001), but only the SSC difference remained significant after age adjustment (p = 0.017). For 3-class classification, the CNN using FLIO achieved the highest AUROC (0.60 {+/-} 0.04), compared with 0.51 {+/-} 0.03 for an age-only classifier. ResNet-18 and XGBoost showed similar performance. Binary classification of normal vs. diabetic participants yielded AUROC 0.67 {+/-} 0.04 (CNN), 0.64 {+/-} 0.04 (ResNet-18), and 0.62 {+/-} 0.04 (XGBoost). All three FLIO models exceeded the age-only classifier in all T2DM classification tasks, whereas adding age to the FLIO models did not improve model performance. ConclusionsFLIO-derived {tau}CMM maps capture retinal signals associated with diabetes status that exceed what age alone provides, but yield modest classification performance with current artificial intelligence models. These findings highlight both the potential and the challenges of using FLIO for early metabolic screening and monitoring, informing future development of clinically applicable imaging biomarkers.

research.abstract: Tetrigidae is an early-branching family of Caelifera whose species live on damp ground, feed largely on mosses, algae and detritus, and often show wing and pronotum polymorphism. Which chemosensory and detoxification genes underlie this lifestyle is unknown. We generated an Oxford Nanopore PCR-cDNA transcriptome from a pooled sample of adult Hyboella guangxiensis (4.25 million full-length reads) and used it, together with protein homology, to filter the 17,996 machine-learning gene models of its chromosome-level genome to 15,338 supported genes without loss of BUSCO completeness. For nine families (OBP, CSP, IR, SNMP, P450, CCE, GST, UGT, ABC), full-length transcripts corrected 28 of 447 loci, including split and fused models, and brought protein lengths into agreement with orthologs of the sister species Bolivaritettix circocephalus (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.00066). research.abstract: Abstract Background Retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are the most common findings on fundus photographs of older adults, yet their frequency, correlates and visual consequences have been estimated in separate samples. We compared them in a national survey that graded both from the same images. Methods We analyzed 5593 adults aged ≥40 years in the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2005–2008 with photographs gradable for both conditions. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence, fitted identically specified logistic models for retinopathy (participants with diabetes) and AMD (full sample), and compared presenting visual impairment (better-eye acuity worse than 20/40) and self-rated vision across four groups: neither condition, retinopathy only, AMD only, and both. Results Retinopathy was more prevalent than AMD (9.54% [95% confidence interval (CI) 8.52–10.56] vs 6.52% [5.54–7.50]); AMD overtook it only from age 70 years. In participants with diabetes, retinopathy was associated with HbA1c (odds ratio [OR] 1.54 per percentage point; 1.33–1.78) and male sex (1.54; 1.10–2.17). AMD was associated with age (OR 1.09 per year; 1.07–1.11) and was less common in non-Hispanic Black adults (0.48; 0.33–0.71). Presenting impairment affected 4.91% of participants with neither condition, 7.09% with retinopathy only, 14.57% with AMD only and 26.15% with both. After age adjustment, impairment remained associated with AMD only (OR 2.23; 1.54–3.23) and both conditions (4.09; 2.28–7.37) but not retinopathy only (1.32; 0.91–1.90). Neither retinopathy nor diabetes was associated with AMD. Self-rated vision agreed poorly with measured impairment (κ = 0.15): only 12% of impaired participants rated their vision poor or very poor. Conclusions Retinopathy is the more frequent retinal finding in US adults aged ≥40 years, but AMD carries more of the measured visual impairment, independently of age. Grading diabetic screening photographs for AMD, and measuring acuity rather than asking about vision, would reach more people who see poorly.

research.abstract: Choanoflagellates, the closest known living relatives of animals, provide a powerful comparative system for investigating the evolution of extracellular morphology and cell behaviour on the animal stem lineage. Although all choanoflagellates share a conserved cellular architecture including a flagellum and collar of microvilli, they display a wide diversity of extracellular structures and behaviours throughout the life cycle. Their extracellular features, historically used for species identification, have long been suspected to reflect a mixture of evolutionary inheritance and ecological plasticity. Yet, the majority of choanoflagellate diversity remains undescribed, and the extent to which their extracellular traits map onto their phylogeny has remained unclear, impeding comparative reconstructions of the evolutionary history of extracellular structures with the earliest animals. Here, we integrate super-resolution fluorescence imaging, electron microscopy and transcriptomic analysis to characterize the extracellular structures and behaviours across both currently described lineages of choanoflagellates (Craspedida and Acanthoecida), by studying pairs of closely related species in conjunction with novel isolates representing previously unexplored clades. Our results reveal strong conservation of extracellular morphology between close relatives, whereas deeper evolutionary distances uncover unexpected innovations, such as sheath-like layers, bipartite thecae, crawling stages and atypical inverted division patterns. Furthermore, the inclusion of early-branching taxa sister to the loricates supports the hypothesis that the silicified extracellular lorica is a derived trait rather than an ancestral feature. Together, our findings suggest that the last choanoflagellate common ancestor possessed an organic non-silicified extracellular covering composed of one or more layers and that it was capable of both swimming and crawling behaviours, refining the cellular context from which animals evolved.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Marine sponges (phylum Porifera) are a highly diverse and polymorphic group of marine invertebrates whose taxonomic delimitation is often challenging due to high intraspecific variability and the scarcity of diagnostic morphological characters. Their close association with microbial symbionts also makes them an important source of secondary metabolites, some of which may contribute to sponge colouration. Here, we use morphological characters, molecular phylogenetic markers, and 16S metabarcoding of the symbiont community to understand speciation in a common Mediterranean sponge lineage. We collected 43 specimens of the genus Suberites from the Mediterranean Sea and the North and South Atlantic Oceans, between 55– 150 m depths, and sequenced two barcoding genes, cytochrome c oxidase I and 28S rDNA, as well as studied their spicular complements. We identified five closely-related species: S. domuncula , S. ficus/pagurorum , S. dandelenae , S. ambulodomus , and a new species of Suberites from the Balearic Islands, Suberites sp. nov. The latter represents a potential new pseudo-cryptic species closely related to S. domuncula , because of their strong morphological and molecular affinities. The potential new Mediterranean species exhibits six colour morphotypes (yellow, gray, orange, brown, red, and blue), and the microbiome analyses of the symbiotic communities revealed significant differences in bacterial community composition among colour morphotypes, specially of bacteria that produce different pigments which potentially give the sponge is colouration. These results provide valuable insights into species boundaries and evolutionary relationships within the genus Suberites and support a role for the microbiome in sponge colouration.

research.abstract: Abstract Objective To describe the role of hysterectomy in modifying the major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Data sources PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect were searched from database inception to March 10, 2026. Study eligibility criteria Full-text randomized controlled trials, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case series, and experimental studies reporting new-onset cardiovascular events, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, or other metabolic effects following hysterectomy were eligible. Reviews and book chapters were excluded. Study appraisal and synthesis methods Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by multiple reviewers with conflicts resolved by consensus. Cohort study quality was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; a modified version assessed cross-sectional studies. Meta-analyses were performed using a generic inverse-variance random-effects model for each outcome, stratified by study design (cross-sectional versus cohort) and effect measure (adjusted odds ratio, adjusted hazard ratio, or relative risk). Narrative synthesis was performed for outcomes not meeting criteria for meta-analysis. Results Twenty studies (11 cohort, 8 cross-sectional, 1 mixed design) were included after screening 18,337 records from four databases. Hysterectomy was associated with significantly increased risk of hypertension (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.32, 95% confidence interval 1.18– 1.48; cohort hazard ratio 1.19, 95% confidence interval 1.09–1.30), diabetes (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.11–1.32; cohort hazard ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.13–1.29), hyperlipidemia (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.13–1.29), obesity (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.03–1.50), and metabolic syndrome (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.08–1.44). Conclusions Hysterectomy is associated with increased risk of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and metabolic syndrome, key modifiable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Active cardiovascular risk assessment and follow-up may be warranted for women who undergo hysterectomy, particularly at a young age.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND Active case finding (ACF) in India screens large populations to find few cases. AI-NETRA predicts neighbourhood-level tuberculosis (TB) risk from routine notification data and generates field microplans. OBJECTIVE To compare the yield and efficiency of AI-guided and standard ACF, and frontline acceptability. DESIGN Prospective quasi-experimental evaluation in four TB Units of Pune district, comparing two-week AI-guided sweeps (April to May 2026) with the routine campaign in the same units (December 2024 to January 2025). Primary endpoint: bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB per persons screened; secondary: all-forms yield, presumptive yield, referral precision, number needed to screen (NNS) and cost per case. Acceptability: 16 focus groups (n=100) and a survey of 101 ASHAs. RESULTS AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and confirmed 10 pulmonary cases, against 9 among 177,322 in the standard campaign (rate ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.09 to 8.29); NNS was 6,610 versus 19,702 and cost per case 66% lower. All-forms detection did not differ (15 versus 32; RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.39); the standard campaign had mobile X-ray. 96% of ASHAs reported finding the same presumptive cases while screening fewer people. CONCLUSION Geospatial targeting raised confirmed yield per person and lowered NNS; total detection did not differ. A concurrent, like-for-like trial is warranted.

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. Our findings underscore the critical need to integrate WGS into TB surveillance and control programmes in Pakistan to guide targeted interventions and curb the spread of resistant strains. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62482-7.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila , and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris , those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

research.abstract: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). Methods: Urine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. Results: Positive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). Conclusion: Three distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Clp proteases are central to bacterial proteostasis, yet our biochemical understanding of actinobacterial Clp enzymes derives almost entirely from mycobacteria, where their essentiality complicates efforts to understand their physiological behavior. Here, we reconstitute and biochemically characterize the ClpCP1P2 protease from Corynebacterium glutamicum , a genetically tractable actinobacterium in which clpC and clpX are non-essential. We find that, as in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , ClpP1 and ClpP2 are individually inactive and form an active peptidase only when stabilized by ATP-bound ClpC or acyldepsipeptide antibiotics, with further stimulation by N-blocked peptide agonists. However, C. glutamicum ClpCP1P2 exhibits faster kinetics and greater conformational stability than its mycobacterial orthologs, proteolyzing full-length substrates rapidly without requiring peptide agonists. We additionally show that the anti-mycobacterial antibiotics rufomycin and cyclomarin A bind the C. glutamicum ClpC N-terminal domain, exert substrate-specific effects on proteolysis, and impair C. glutamicum growth. The ability of these compounds to elicit toxicity through a non-essential target suggests that they act via gain-of-function dysregulation rather than simple inhibition. Together, our results validate C. glutamicum as a tractable model for interrogating Actinomycetota Clp proteases. IMPORTANCE Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains one of the world’s deadliest bacterial pathogens and its Clp proteases are promising targets for new antibiotics. However, because these enzymes are essential in mycobacteria, it is difficult to study their physiological roles. Here, we show that the Clp protease of Corynebacterium glutamicum , a non-pathogenic relative in which the unfoldase ClpC is dispensable, shares the core assembly and regulatory features of its mycobacterial counterpart while being more stable and catalytically faster. Anti-mycobacterial ClpC-targeting antibiotics also act on this system, supporting a model in which they cause protease dysregulation rather than simple inhibition. These findings establish a genetically tractable model for dissecting actinobacterial Clp protease mechanisms and antibiotic action. They may also inform strategies for engineering regulated protein degradation in C. glutamicum , an important industrial microbe.

research.abstract: Background and Aims: Preclinical studies implicate NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which drives release of interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18, in vascular inflammation and atherosclerosis, and selective NLRP3 inhibitors are now in clinical development. However, whether lowering NLRP3 activity reduces coronary artery disease (CAD) risk in humans is unknown. We used human genetics to estimate this effect and its mediating pathways. Methods: A genetic NLRP3 activity score was derived by combining the effects of eight cis-NLRP3 variants on NLRP3 expression and three inflammatory biomarkers: C-reactive protein, glycoprotein acetylation, and neutrophil count. The score was validated against circulating interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18. Drug-target Mendelian randomization was used to estimate its association with CAD, cardiometabolic traits and other diseases studied in NLRP3 inhibitor trials. Mediation by cardiometabolic risk factors was quantified using the product-of-coefficients method. Results: A lower genetically proxied NLRP3 activity score was associated with lower circulating interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18, but with higher CAD risk (OR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.02 - 1.45, P = 0.032). It was also associated with higher systolic blood pressure, apolipoprotein B levels, and type 2 diabetes risk, which together mediated an estimated 87% of the association with CAD. The residual direct association with CAD was attenuated (OR = 1.03, 95% CI 0.85 - 1.24, P = 0.79). In contrast, a lower score was nominally associated with lower risk of gout, pericarditis, and Parkinson's disease. Conclusions: Lifelong lower genetically proxied NLRP3 activity was associated with higher CAD risk, largely mediated by adverse cardiometabolic effects, with no evidence of protection after accounting for them. These findings do not provide genetic support for lowering NLRP3 activity to reduce CAD risk.

research.abstract: Background. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a snapshot: a single measurement interpreted against a population threshold. Repeated (longitudinal) measurements, however, may reveal an individual's typical level and how it changes over time. Extracting this information is challenging when measurements are sparse and biological fluctuations may resemble sustained changes. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), we investigated whether individual glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) trajectories improved the prediction of incident diabetes beyond the most recent measurement, whether they were associated with incident diabetes, and how reliably they could be estimated. Methods. In this secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, we analysed venous HbA1c measured approximately every four years in ELSA, with a longer final interval of about seven years. A linear mixed model estimated each person's usual HbA1c level and rate of change (personal slope) from their measurements before each diabetes-free health visit, with model parameters estimated in other participants (cross-fitting). We derived four longitudinal features: deviation from the person's usual level, personal slope, change since the last measurement, and the forecast probability that the next HbA1c reaches the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. We evaluated the associations of these features with incident diabetes and their incremental predictive value beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors in internal, cross-fitted validation, compared predictive performance with a self-supervised Transformer, and modelled within-person variation as serially correlated drift (an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) to assess how reliably personal slopes can be recovered under different measurement schedules. Results. The analysis included 5,828 diabetes-free baseline visits from 3,603 participants, of which 234 were followed by incident diabetes. Neither the engineered longitudinal features nor a Transformer that also used additional clinical variables improved discrimination beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors (difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, {Delta}AUC, -0.002 to +0.010; all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] including zero). The estimated personal slope was nevertheless associated with incident diabetes after adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age and other clinical factors (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] 1.18, 95% CI 1.02--1.36, and 1.39, 1.11--1.74, among visits with at least two earlier HbA1c values), whereas deviation from the person's usual level was not (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.81--1.21). In the drift model, serially correlated fluctuations accounted for 77--81% of residual within-person variance, although the estimated temporal structure was sensitive to the treatment of the first HbA1c values at or above the diagnostic threshold. Under this model, persistent individual trends were difficult to distinguish from slowly varying fluctuations: with the intercept-slope correlation set to zero, estimated and underlying slopes correlated weakly for four-yearly measurements over up to 12 years (r [≤] 0.26), and more frequent measurements improved this little. Conclusions. Estimated personal HbA1c slopes carried adjusted prognostic information beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical factors, but longitudinal features, including those learned by a Transformer, did not clearly improve prediction. The drift model suggests that slowly varying within-person fluctuations may limit the reliable estimation of individual slopes from sparse measurements, and that longer observation histories are more informative than more frequent measurement. Whether personal laboratory histories improve prediction depends not only on their association with disease, but also on how reliably individual change can be recovered from the available measurements.

research.abstract: Aims Approaches to meaningfully identify individuals with differing prognosis at type 2 diabetes diagnosis are lacking. We aimed to assess whether QDiabetes, a validated routine clinical feature-based model to predict risk of type 2 diabetes onset, could be applied at the point of diagnosis to identify people with atypical type 2 diabetes with differing risk of complications and treatment requirements. Methods We included adults newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2013-2023 in population-representative UK primary care data (Clinical Practice Research Datalink). Individuals with low predicted QDiabetes risk ([≤]5.6%) were classified as atypical type 2 diabetes and matched up to 1:4 by age, sex and calendar year to typical type 2 diabetes (QDiabetes risk >5.6%). We compared 10-year risks of microvascular, macrovascular, acute complications, mortality and glucose-lowering treatment initiation. For complications, multivariable Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs), adjusting for age, sex, year of diagnosis, ethnicity, deprivation and baseline HbA1c. Results Of 276,117 individuals newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, 30,397 (11.0%) were classified as atypical type 2 diabetes using our approach. Compared with the wider typical type 2 diabetes population (n=245,720; 89.0%), they were younger (54 vs 60 years), leaner (26.4 vs 34.0 kg/m2) and had higher HbA1c at diagnosis (68.0 vs 60.0 mmol/mol). In matched analyses, the atypical type 2 diabetes group had a higher risk of severe retinopathy (aHR 1.33, 95% CI 1.23-1.44), similar risk of severe neuropathy (aHR 0.92, 0.84-1.01), and lower risk of severe nephropathy (aHR 0.81, 0.73-0.90). Despite lower predicted baseline cardiovascular risk in those with atypical type 2 diabetes, risks of myocardial infarction (aHR 0.99, 0.89-1.11) and stroke (aHR 0.92, 0.81-1.04) were similar, while heart failure risk was lower (aHR 0.72, 0.67-0.78). Atypical type 2 diabetes was also associated with higher risks of diabetic ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycaemia, non-cardiovascular mortality and insulin initiation. Conclusion Type 2 diabetes onset risk prediction models used at the point of diagnosis may represent a pragmatic approach to identify people with an atypical type 2 diabetes phenotype. Despite fewer conventional risk factors, the phenotype identified had a poor prognosis and could provide a practical target for personalised type 2 diabetes management to reduce risk of long-term complications.

research.abstract: Coptis species belong to the Ranunculaceae family and have important pharmacological activity because their rhizomes are rich in isoquinoline alkaloids. However, the genome evolution and species relationships of Coptis remain poorly understood. Here, we report high-quality chromosome-level genome assemblies of four representative Coptis species (C. chinensis, C. deltoidea, C. omeiensis, and C. teeta). We found that the evolution of this group was strongly affected by geological events, especially the uplift of the Tibetan Plateau and the collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates. The triploid C. deltoidea exhibited striking B subgenome expression dominance, while C. omeiensis showed extensive tandem duplication of NLR disease-resistance genes. Rhizome branching and swelling were closely associated with the activation of brassinosteroid biosynthesis and signaling pathways. Key gene families involved in alkaloid biosynthesis were significantly expanded in Coptis and were mainly highly expressed in the rhizome. Multiple transcription factor families, including MYB, bHLH, and ERF, were identified as candidate regulatory factors associated with alkaloid biosynthesis. We further constructed the first public multi-omics database for Coptis. This study provides key genomic resources for understanding Coptis evolution, adaptation, and molecular breeding.

research.abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major challenge in tuberculosis control, and the occurrence of resistance in patients without any prior treatment history raises concern about the transmission of resistant strains within the community. We report the case of a 63-year-old woman presenting with cough for more than two months, marked weight loss, and intermittent fever, without any previous tuberculosis treatment or known contact with a tuberculosis patient. She had a history of diabetes mellitus. Physical examination revealed bronchial breath sounds with rhonchi, and chest radiography revealed infiltration at the right upper lung apex. Rapid molecular testing detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with resistance to rifampicin, and second-line drug susceptibility testing further revealed additional resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolone, and ethionamide, leading to a diagnosis of primary pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis. Random blood glucose was elevated and was managed with insulin, while mild hypochromic anaemia was managed with iron supplementation. The patient received bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, and remained clinically stable without significant adverse effects after one week of therapy. This case highlights the importance of vigilance for primary drug-resistant tuberculosis and the role of rapid molecular testing in early diagnosis and appropriate treatment selection.

research.abstract: Abstract Eco-evolutionary feedbacks are typically thought to require an ecological change driving Darwinian selection. However, ecology can drive other evolutionary mechanisms too. In many microbial species mutation rates are elevated at low population density, mediated by nutrient availability and reactive oxygen species (ROS). These findings from monoculture populations led us to hypothesise that the presence and density of a cohabiting species will also affect mutation rates. Using Escherichia coli as a focal species we explore the mutational effects on both parties of co-culture with either Enterococcus faecalis or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These species co-occur in multiple clinical settings and have different abilities to degrade ROS. In both co-culture systems we find evidence that the presence of a stronger ROS degrader reduces mutation rates in the weaker ROS degrading species. At the same time increasing population density of the weaker ROS degrader increases mutation rates in the stronger ROS degrading species. Simultaneous mutation rate estimation in co-cultured species raises multiple experimental challenges addressed here. Despite these challenges, we find evidence for a novel form of eco-evo feedback in which the environment shapes the supply of mutational variation to the population. This in turn feeds back to alter the chance of evolutionary rescue for one species or another during a subsequent environmental change. Such effects potentially matter not only for our fundamental understanding of the interplay between ecology and evolution, but for the treatment of polymicrobial infections in which rates of resistance evolution may be altered by the cross-species mutational effects of cohabiting species.

research.abstract: Abstract Codon-based maximum likelihood models are the workhorse of molecular selection analysis, yet standard workflows assume that the input sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree are known without error. In practice, heuristic aligners ignore the genetic code and phylogeny, which packs non-homologous codons into shared columns across insertion-deletion loops and inflates gene-wide false-positive rates above 80%. This sequential division of labor is statistically suboptimal and computationally wasteful. Here, we present WALRUS ( W heatstone A lignment and L ikelihood R ate U nification for S election), a unified engine in H y P hy 3 ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ) that maps unaligned coding sequences to a coordinate-consistent selection atlas in one run. From a single Inside–Outside likelihood table, the pipeline repairs reading frames, co-estimates a codon alignment and Ohmic reticulate network, models directional base-composition drift, and evaluates eight selection tests (BUSTED-E, aBSREL, RELAX, FEL, dFEL, MEME, Contrast-FEL, and PRIME). Across 10,020 simulated alignments, WALRUS recovers 94.6% of true columns on the 800 INDELible replicates and cuts indel-driven false positives from 44.7%– 58.1% to 4.4% under BUSTED (21.1%– 21.4% to 1.4% under BUSTED-E). Under Zipfian indel saturation, false positives drop four-fold (33.3%– 83.3% to 17.0%– 20.5%), while 11, 190 avian orthogroup runs execute 6.6–35.8-fold faster and cut housekeeping false positives 13-fold (28-fold on ultraconserved genes) proteome-wide.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum–culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.

research.abstract: Abstract Background The HSP70 family maintains cellular proteostasis and mediates vertebrate responses to environmental stress. The Chinese alligator ( Alligator sinensis ), an ectothermic crocodilian, undergoes winter dormancy characterized by cessation of feeding, reduced activity, and metabolic depression. However, the evolutionary patterns of the HSP70 family across vertebrates and their potential relevance to winter dormancy in crocodilians remain poorly understood. We characterized the HSP70 family across 24 vertebrate species, focusing on the molecular evolution of HSPA12A along crocodilian lineages and its seasonal expression in the hypothalamus of the Chinese alligator. Results Using HMMER- and BLAST-based searches, we identified 355 HSP70 family members, with 11–28 members per species. Phylogenetic, synteny, and subcellular localization analyses indicated that the family is broadly conserved but exhibits subfamily- and lineage-associated divergence. Under two foreground schemes in which the terminal branches of two winter-dormant crocodilians or all four crocodilian species were jointly designated as foreground, HSPA12A showed an elevated relative evolutionary rate and significant evidence of positive selection. HyPhy aBSREL supported episodic diversifying selection on the A. sinensis HSPA12A terminal branch. Public RNA-seq data showed that HSPA12A expression was highest in the hypothalamus among sampled female tissues and was higher in winter than in summer (600.0 and 329.2 TPM, respectively). Western blotting and immunofluorescence analyses showed descriptive differences between the examined specimens, with higher HSPA12A protein abundance and a higher density of cells double-positive for anti-HSPA12A antibody immunoreactivity and NeuN in winter. Because each RNA-seq, western blotting, and immunofluorescence comparison included only one biological specimen per season, these observations were treated as descriptive, and no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Conclusions The vertebrate HSP70 family is broadly conserved but shows differentiation among subfamilies and lineages. The evolutionary analyses indicate a broader crocodilian-lineage-associated pattern of HSPA12A evolution that cannot be attributed specifically to winter dormancy. Separately, the descriptive transcriptomic and preliminary protein-level observations provide a basis for considering HSPA12A as a candidate for further investigation in relation to winter physiology in the Chinese alligator. These findings do not establish winter dormancy as the selective driver of HSPA12A evolution, and its biological function and causal role remain to be determined.

research.abstract: Camelids have evolved remarkable physiological adaptations enabling survival in extreme desert environments, yet the genomic basis of these traits remains incompletely understood. We conducted a comparative genomic analysis across eleven mammalian species, including three Old World camels, four New World camels, two additional artiodactyls (pig, cattle), and two outgroups (human, mouse), to identify lineage-specific molecular signatures of adaptation. Using OrthoFinder, we constructed orthologous gene families and identified 11,861 single-copy orthologs across all species. We detected significant copy-number changes in cytochrome P450 gene families, with expansion of CYP2J and contraction of CYP4F in the camelid ancestor, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory eicosanoid signaling. Branch-site analyses identified 47 high-confidence positively selected genes in Old World camels, including HACD3, a fatty acid elongation enzyme harboring an ultraconserved substitution (D270N). Structural modeling and conservation analysis suggest that this substitution may hypothetically alter protein conformation, but this prediction awaits experimental validation. Tissue-specific RNA-seq analysis confirmed that HACD3 is expressed in camel kidney and liver, tissues central to lipid metabolism and water conservation. Systematic screening for inactivating mutations identified ten high-confidence pseudogenized genes, including CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, enriched in lipid metabolism and epidermal pathways. The adaptive significance of these losses is currently hypothetical and inferred from homologous gene studies in mice and humans; because some of the cited genes are paralogs rather than orthologs, and because mouse and human phenotypes may not transfer to camels, these inferences are hypothesis-generating only and do not establish camel gene function. Experimental validation confirmed pseudogenization of TAS2R16, and cell-based calcium-signalling assays showed that the camel receptor fails to respond to salicin. This establishes loss of receptor function but not its adaptive significance; both dietary-breadth and neutral (relaxed-selection or drift) explanations remain compatible with the data. For CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, functional consequences in camels remain unverified and require camel-specific experimental validation. Collectively, these results provide a comprehensive framework of gene family evolution, positive selection, and gene loss underlying desert adaptation in camelids, while highlighting that expression patterns are correlative only and do not demonstrate that the identified variants alter protein function or physiology.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Dosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. Methodology A pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to 10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80–125% of adult area under the concentration–time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. Results Proposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10–14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25–39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6–24.9 kg. Conclusions A harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed. Author Summary Leprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available. In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care. This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.

research.abstract: IntroductionAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) to first line antibiotics for pneumonia is a major global health problem, and AMR-attributable deaths are prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa. Improved data on how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource limited settings is crucial. The nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their resistome, the genetic determinants of AMR. No study has explored whether human resistome composition in children with pneumonia is associated with health outcomes. This study will examine whether antibiotic treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired nasopharyngeal resistome in children, and whether this is associated with re-hospitalisation. MethodsThis is an observational case-control study, that will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months from four groups in Blantyre, Malawi: healthy children in the community (healthy community), children with pneumonia treated in the community (community pneumonia), children hospitalised with pneumonia (hospital pneumonia) and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia (re-hospitalised pneumonia). Nasopharyngeal swabs will be taken at recruitment and 3-month follow-up study visits for metagenomic sequencing to characterise the nasopharyngeal microbiome and resistome; urine samples will be taken at recruitment for an antibiotic activity bioassay. Socio-demographic data, co-morbidities, pneumonia severity, antibiotic exposure and health outcomes will be recorded. AnalysisCross-sectional comparisons between groups at recruitment will examine whether nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) composition differs by pneumonia severity, antibiotic and healthcare exposure. Longitudinal comparisons within groups will assess the dynamics of NPR composition over time. The study is powered to detect a medium effect size (Cohens D = 0.505) change in the relative abundance of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) between all four groups. Primary outcomes are the difference in beta diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index), and relative abundance of ARG classes in the NPR. The primary objectives are to estimate the difference in diversity and relative abundance of the NPR between hospitalised pneumonia participants when compared to 1) healthy community and 2) community pneumonia participants, and to investigate whether participants re-hospitalised with pneumonia within a 3-month period have a persistent hospital-acquired NPR pattern. Ethics and disseminationThe study has been approved by the Kamuzu University of Heath Sciences Research Ethics Committee (KUREC, formerly Malawi College of Medicine Research Ethics Committee; Ref: P.10/24-1200) and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Committee (LSTM REC; Ref: 24-076). Trial registration numberISRCTN64027792 STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDYO_ST_ABSStrengthsC_ST_ABSO_LIStudy design that uses metagenomic deep sequencing to enable direct, concurrent comparison of nasopharyngeal microbiome (NPM) and resistome (NPR) composition between community and hospitalised paediatric populations with pneumonia in a resource-limited setting. C_LIO_LIData on reported and urinary bioassay-detected antibiotic use prior to, and throughout the study, enabling detailed examination of antibiotic selective pressure on the NPR. C_LIO_LIInvestigation of the association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes from pneumonia. C_LI LimitationsO_LILimitations to this study include few sampling time points (two for community pneumonia and three for hospitalised pneumonia), which may not fully capture the impact of antibiotic exposure; the potential for residual confounding following adjustment for known potential confounders (e.g. age, sex, co-morbidities, household exposure to smoke and breastfeeding) in the association between resistome composition and adverse clinical outcomes, for which the authors have detailed statistical analysis measures; and ability to only determine association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes, rather than causal inference, due to the case-control study design. C_LI SUMMARYO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSThe nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance in children. Studies of nasopharyngeal microbiome composition have shown association with paediatric pneumonia severity and mortality. What this study addsThis study will describe nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) evolution under selective pressure of antibiotics and hospitalisation for paediatric pneumonia, and explore whether NPR composition is associated with health outcomes in a resource-limited setting. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThis exploratory study could inform larger scale observational studies to examine the association between antibiotic resistance and health outcomes, by defining high-risk nasopharyngeal resistome composition, helping to determine the required sample size and contributing open-source bioinformatic pipelines. The study could also inform research for public health interventions, including antibiotic stewardship.

research.abstract: Darwin described the somersaulting behavior of pigeons as "one of the most remarkable inherited habits ever recorded", yet its molecular basis remained unknown. We show that somersaulting pigeon brains exhibit mitochondrial redox dysfunction and identify an 11-bp frameshifting deletion in GLRX2 , a mitochondrial redox enzyme, that abolishes protein function and is highly-enriched in two independently selected breeds. GLRX2 deficiency in mice and zebrafish recapitulates mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress and impaired motor coordination seen in pigeons. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identifies cerebellar Golgi and Purkinje cells as selectively vulnerable, with disrupted inhibitory signaling and synaptic remodeling. These findings demonstrate how relaxation of purifying selection during domestication can expose a deleterious mitochondrial variant to artificial selection, allowing gene loss to serve as a substrate for behavioral evolution.

research.abstract: Abstract Bacteria engage in many cooperative behaviours which provide benefits to other cells in the population. Lab experiments have suggested that these costly behaviours can be favoured by kin selection due to the benefits they provide to closely related cells. However, we know much less about the role of kin selection in natural populations. Here, we used two complementary methods to measure and compare kin selected signatures of cooperation in 19 species of bacteria found in the guts of honey bees. We used bioinformatic tools to count the number (and proportion) of genes for cooperative traits in a genome, and used molecular population genetics to measure how natural selection is acting on those genes. We found evidence for a consistent signature of kin selection for cooperation on genes controlling cooperative traits across species. Genes for cooperative traits had more non-synonymous relative to synonymous polymorphism than genes for private traits, had more protein-changing mutations and more codons under positive selection, and were lost more often. From this signature, we estimate an average relatedness of 0.73 between interacting cells. However, we found no evidence supporting the prediction that this signature varies with relatedness estimated from metagenomes. These patterns suggest that whilst genes for cooperative traits are undergoing kin selection in natural populations, there may be other factors influencing how the action of kin selection varies across species. Impact Statement Bacteria cooperate by secreting molecules that benefit other cells, such as enzymes that break down food and molecules that take up iron. Kin selection theory predicts that genes for these cooperative traits are under weaker selection than genes for private traits, which benefit only the cell that makes them. We tested this prediction across 19 species of bacteria from the honey bee gut. As predicted, we found that genes for cooperative traits had more non-synonymous relative to synonymous polymorphism than those for private traits. Between strains of the same species, genes for cooperative traits had more protein-changing mutations and more positively selected codons, and were lost more often. However, these differences did not vary across species with relatedness estimated from metagenomes. One possible reason is that bacteria interact in small patches of the gut, so our whole-gut metagenomic estimates of relatedness may not be accurate.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Synonymous codon usage bias (CUB) provides a complementary perspective on molecular variation, but its relationship with morphological diversity in rapidly radiating plant lineages remains poorly understood. We investigated this relationship in Thelypteridaceae by integrating chloroplast phylogenomics, codon usage analyses, and published descriptions of lamina base architecture. A phylogeny based on 31 shared protein‐coding genes provided the evolutionary framework for 37 plastome accessions, including two outgroups. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) revealed three major codon usage groupings (Types A–C) that partly differed from the chloroplast phylogeny, with Types A and C corresponding descriptively to contrasting lamina base forms. A focused comparison of 27 accessions and eight genes retained this Type A–Type C separation. Although ENC, PR2, and neutrality plots showed broadly similar overall patterns between the types, gene‐wise analyses highlighted ndhJ, psaA, and psbD, and protein‐guided codon alignments reproduced their type‐specific synonymous third‐position counts. These complementary observations support a relationship between chloroplast codon usage variation and frond architecture in the sampled taxa. They identify candidate photosynthesis‐related loci and provide a basis for testing the evolutionary and functional processes underlying this relationship.

research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects the lungs and causes the disease tuberculosis, which the World Health Organization estimates causes 1 million deaths across the globe annually. Emergence of drug resistance has lessened the effectiveness and requires a longer duration of treatment. Bedaquiline was approved by the FDA in 2012 to treat multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis cases when no other treatment was viable. TBAJ-587, a derivative of Bedaquiline, has been found to be more effective at treating multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis, and has fewer adverse effects. The aim of this project was to test if strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that have a mutation in Rv0678 causing overexpression of the MmpS5L5 efflux pump will evolve high-level resistance to TBAJ-587 at a higher frequency than wild-type strains. This was done by growing a wild-type M. tuberculosis strain and a ∆Rv0678 mutant on plates of 7H11 agar containing increasing concentrations of TBAJ-587, then selecting isolates and confirming resistance using an anti-microbial susceptibility assay to determine the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration of the isolated strains. 72 strains from the wild-type background were assayed, and 114 from the ∆Rv0678 background were assayed. The resistant ∆Rv0678 strains tended to have higher minimum inhibitory concentrations that the resistant WT strains. Mutations in the WT strains were found throughout Rv0678, and D28, E6, A62 and I66 mutations in atpE, as well as L168 in atpB. Similar atpE mutations were found in ∆Rv0678, with the addition of mutations in A63 of atpE.
